transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a long story, I suppose. I haven't been feeling quite right for a while now, just sort of heavy, you know? Like everything takes so much effort, even just getting out of bed or making a cup of tea. But what really scared me... what finally made me pick up the phone and make this appointment, even though I hate bothering people... is my thoughts. Lately, when I lay down at night, I keep thinking... I keep thinking it would just be such a relief if I didn't wake up the next morning. Just... slip away quietly, without any fuss. Now, I want to be clear, I haven't tried to hurt myself or anything like that. I don't have a plan or... or pills hidden away. I wouldn't do that to my family. But the thought is just there, hovering, you know? Like a dark cloud that whispers how much easier it would all be if it just stopped. And it frightened me, having those thoughts, because I used to love the mornings, but now... now I just wish they wouldn't come.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the heaviness and the thoughts about not wanting to wake up?

Well, if I really sit down and look back at the calendar... I'd say it's been about four months now. Yes, four months. It all started right around the time my aunt came to live with us. You see, she just couldn't manage on her own anymore, bless her heart, and well, family is family, so of course we had to take her in. But oh, it was such a big adjustment for everyone. I really thought I could handle it just fine—I’ve always been the one to take care of things, you know? 

But right after she got settled in the spare room, that's when this... this awful heaviness just started creeping into my bones. At first, I honestly just thought I was worn out from moving all her boxes and rearranging the house. We had to move the whole living room around just to fit her favorite recliner, and I'm not as young as I used to be. But the heaviness, it never went away, it just got deeper and deeper. 

And then, maybe a few weeks after she moved in, that's when those nighttime thoughts started happening. So yes, four whole months of this. Four months of going to sleep just hoping I wouldn't have to do it all over again the next day. It’s a long time to feel like that, isn't it? I kept waiting to just bounce back like I used to, thinking maybe once we got into a routine with her it would lift, but the days just keep blurring together and that dark cloud just stays right there.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these feelings started?

Well, doctor, that's... that's a sad thing to admit, really. Because if you asked anyone who knows me, they'd tell you I used to be quite the busy bee. My days were just full of things I loved doing. Like my painting... I used to look forward to my watercolors so much. I have this little setup right by the kitchen window—the light hits just perfectly there in the late afternoons, you see, right around four o'clock. I'd paint little birds, mostly, or whatever flowers were blooming out front in the beds. I just loved mixing the colors on this little plastic palette I got at the craft store... but lately, I just... I just leave my things sitting there. The easel is still up, probably collecting dust by now, and I look at it and I just can't make myself care. It feels like such a mountain to climb just to think about filling up the little water cup. 

And it’s the exact same story with my dance class. Oh, I used to love Tuesday mornings! A group of us would go down to the community center for line dancing. We'd dance to those old country songs, and I even bought these special shoes with suede on the bottoms so you can slide real nice on the wood floor without scuffing it up. But now... I haven't been in months. I just look at those shoes sitting in the bottom of the closet and think, what's the point? I can't muster up a single ounce of joy for the music anymore, let alone the dancing. 

Even just walking with the ladies... I used to do that every Thursday, rain or shine, unless it was pouring, of course. We’d do a whole big loop around the park, catching up on all the neighborhood news, seeing whose grandkids were doing what, looking at the gardens. They still call me, bless them, they leave voicemails asking if I'm coming out with them, but I just let the phone ring. I tell myself I'll go, I really do, but then the time comes and... I just don't care about the walk, or the chatting, or any of it. It's just like all the color has washed right out of everything.
Do you feel guilty about having these thoughts of not wanting to wake up?

Oh, doctor, the guilt... the guilt is just awful. It really eats me alive. I do feel bad about those nighttime thoughts, yes, because I know how much that would hurt my family, but... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, the thing that really brings on the worst of the guilt, the thing that just makes me sick to my stomach, is how I've been feeling about my aunt. 

I mean, like I said before, family is family. My own mother, rest her soul, she always taught us that you take care of your own, no questions asked. You open your door. But lately, with this terrible heaviness making everything so hard... sometimes I just get so bone-tired, or I find myself getting just plain annoyed with her. She'll call out asking for a fresh glass of water, or she'll need help finding the television remote—she's always losing that little black remote down the side of the recliner cushions, you know, the one we had to move the whole room for—and I just feel this awful, ugly spike of irritation. 

And then, almost immediately, the guilt just crashes right down on me. I start thinking... I start thinking about what kind of a person I must be to feel that way. I tell myself I'm a bad woman. A truly bad, wicked woman for feeling annoyed at an elderly lady who just needs a little help and can't do for herself anymore. I feel like I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I mean, I should be counting my blessings! I should be grateful we have a nice home and a spare room to put her in, but instead, I'm just sitting there at the kitchen table feeling resentful. It’s shameful, it really is. I just sit there and think about how worthless I am for not having a better heart about it all, and how I'm failing everyone by being so ungrateful. It just loops in my head, over and over, how bad I am for feeling annoyed...
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past four months?

Well, my weight... you know, I haven't really stepped on the scale in a while. I used to keep it right there in the bathroom, tucked under the vanity, the one with the little blue dial that my husband bought me years ago. But honestly, I just haven't been paying much attention to it lately. I mean, my clothes seem to fit about the same, maybe a little looser or tighter depending on the day, but nothing that really makes me stop and think, "Oh, I've gained," or "Oh, I've lost." 

It's funny you ask, though, because I used to be so careful about my weight, especially back when I was going to my line dancing classes. I wanted to make sure I could still move around comfortably and not get too winded, you know? But now, with everything going on, with my aunt being here and all this heaviness I've been feeling, keeping track of my weight just hasn't even crossed my mind. I still cook, of course, because my aunt needs her three meals a day, and she’s quite particular about her breakfast—she has to have her oatmeal made with milk, not water, and just a tiny sprinkle of brown sugar. So I'm still in the kitchen, still putting food on the table, but as for me and my own weight... I just couldn't tell you if the numbers have moved one way or the other. I just haven't noticed any big changes, really.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping over the past four months?

Sleep... oh, sleep has just been... well, it's just fine, really. I mean, I haven't noticed any real trouble with it. I go to bed around the same time I always do, usually right after the ten o'clock news finishes up. I like to watch the local broadcast, you know, just to see what the weather is going to do the next day, even though I hardly go out anymore. The meteorologist, the young man with the nice smile, he always does such a good job explaining the radar. Anyway, after that, I make sure the front door is locked, check that the stove is off—I have to check it two or three times just to be absolutely sure, a habit I picked up from my mother—and then I head to bed. 

And once I'm in bed, I just... I sleep. I guess I must be sleeping alright because I don't remember tossing and turning or waking up and looking at the clock at all hours of the night. My husband used to do that, bless him. He'd wake up at two in the morning and go sit in the living room and read his history books. But me, I just pull the covers up, and the next thing I know, it's morning and I have to get up to start the oatmeal for my aunt. So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble sleeping. It's just the usual routine, night in and night out, nothing out of the ordinary at all.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or feeling like it's harder to get things done physically over the past four months?

Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have been moving a bit differently. My husband, bless his heart, he actually brought it up just the other day. We were in the kitchen, and I was trying to get the good china down from the top shelf of the hutch—the set we got for our 25th anniversary, the one with the little gold rim—and he came in and told me that I move like everything takes extra effort now. Like I'm walking through molasses or something. He said I look so heavy when I walk, like just lifting my feet is a chore. 

And, you know, I didn't want to admit it to him right then, because I don't want him worrying, but he's right. Even when I go to the market... oh, the market has become such an ordeal. I used to just zip in and out, you know? Grab my cart, go straight to the produce, pick out the firmest tomatoes, and be done with it. But lately, I'll go down to the Piggly Wiggly—I still go to the one on Elm Street because the produce manager, Mr. Henderson, always makes sure the apples are fresh—and I'll find myself just... standing there. I'll stand right in front of the display, looking at the fruit, and I just can't seem to make my hand reach out and pick up what I came for. It's like my brain knows what to do, but my body just takes so, so long to catch up. I just stand there for the longest time, staring, before I can finally get my arm to move and put a simple bag of carrots in the basket. It’s just so much harder to get anything done.
Do you feel like you have less energy than you used to?

Energy... oh, my goodness, yes. It's just... I really don't know where it all went. Like I was telling you just a minute ago about my sleep, I spend a full night in bed, right? I get my rest, the whole night through, but when I wake up, my body just feels completely worn out. It just doesn't make any sense to me. I used to be up with the sun, ready to tackle the day, get the whole house in order before nine o'clock. 

But now... well, just making that breakfast I told you about, the oatmeal for my aunt, it takes so much out of me. I find myself having to lean against the kitchen counter while the milk heats up because I just don't have the strength to stand there straight. And the laundry! Oh, heavens, the laundry. I have this old wicker basket, the one with the little floral cloth liner that ties at the corners—my daughter bought it for me at a craft fair years ago, such a pretty thing—and just carrying that basket from the bedroom down the hall to the washing machine... it feels like I've run a marathon. It just takes more out of me than it ever should. I actually have to sit down on the edge of the bed and catch my breath before I can even think about pouring the detergent or sorting the whites from the colors. I just don't have the pep I used to have, no matter how much I sleep.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite over the past four months?

Appetite... well, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed much at all. I still eat my regular meals, just like always. It's funny you ask, though, because with how completely exhausted I feel, you'd think I just wouldn't have the stomach for it, but I still get hungry right on schedule. 

Like for breakfast... well, after I make that oatmeal for my aunt, I usually fix myself a slice of toast. Just one slice, usually the honey wheat, toasted right to a nice golden brown. I have this older toaster, a Sunbeam, the chrome kind—they just don't make them like that anymore, do they? It pops up perfect every single time. And I'll put a little butter on it, and maybe some of the strawberry preserves my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, brings over. She makes it from scratch every summer, boils the glass jars and seals them with the wax and everything. She's such a sweet lady, always checking in on me. 

And then for lunch, it's usually just a half a sandwich or a little bowl of soup. Campbell's tomato, mostly, especially when it's damp out. I'll heat it up on the stove—I just refuse to use the microwave for soup, it always gets boiling hot on the edges and stays ice cold in the middle, you know how that goes? And for dinner, well, I still try to make a proper meal, even if it takes me twice as long to stand there and chop the onions now because my arms feel so heavy. I'll do a nice meatloaf or a roast chicken. I always roast a chicken on Sundays, with the carrots and the little red potatoes all tucked around it in the pan to soak up the juices. 

So, yes, I'm still eating just about the exact same amount I always have. My stomach still rumbles right around noon, regular as a clock. I haven't noticed any difference at all in my appetite, really.
Have you had trouble concentrating on things like reading or watching TV over the past four months?

Concentrating... well, let me think about that. No, I really haven't had any trouble with my concentration. I still watch my programs every evening just fine. My husband and I, we sit down right at 7:00 PM on the dot for Wheel of Fortune. We've been watching it for, oh, it must be thirty years now. Vanna always has the most beautiful gowns, doesn't she? I always tell my husband I'd love to know who her designer is, not that a woman my age has anywhere to wear a sequined floor-length dress! But I can follow the puzzles without any trouble at all. In fact, just last night, I solved the bonus puzzle before the contestant even guessed a vowel. It was 'A Walk in the Park.' So I can focus on that just perfectly. 

And as for reading, well, I don't read big thick novels so much, mostly because my eyes get a little tired with these bifocals if the print is too small, but I still read my Reader's Digest from cover to cover. My sister gets me a subscription every year for my birthday, she never forgets. They have those wonderful little stories, you know, the 'Drama in Real Life' section? I read one just yesterday afternoon about a man who got stuck in a terrible snowstorm in his pickup truck for three whole days up in the Dakotas somewhere. I read the entire article in one sitting while I was resting my legs on the sofa. I didn't lose my place or find myself having to reread paragraphs or anything like that. So, no, my mind is still sharp as a tack when it comes to paying attention to my shows and my magazines, even if my body is just dragging behind.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless, or do you feel like you're moving in slow motion most of the time?

Slow motion... well, it's funny you put it exactly that way, because that is exactly what my husband, Arthur, has been saying to me lately. He says I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm walking through molasses or something. And I suppose he's right, though I don't always notice it myself until he points it out. It's just... everything feels so heavy. 

Like the other day, we went down to the Piggly Wiggly—we always go on Tuesdays because they have the senior discount, ten percent off your whole cart, which really adds up when you're buying meat and coffee, you know? Anyway, we were in the produce section, and I needed to get some yellow onions for a pot roast I was planning to make. I like the medium-sized ones, not those giant Spanish onions, they're just too much for the two of us. And I was standing there, just standing in front of the onion bin, and Arthur came up behind me with the cart and said, "Martha, are you going to pick one or are we going to stand here until they sprout?" And I realized I had just been standing there... looking at them. For I don't know how long. I knew what I wanted, I knew I needed to reach out and put three of them in one of those little plastic bags on the roll, but I just... I couldn't seem to make my arm do it right away. 

It's like there's this delay between my brain telling my body to move and my body actually doing it. Even getting up from my recliner in the evening—it's a La-Z-Boy, the kind with the handle on the side, upholstered in this lovely sage green chenille—it takes me three or four tries to rock myself up, and then I just stand there for a minute before I take a step. I'm definitely not fidgety or restless, I can tell you that for sure. If anything, I'm just so terribly slow. It just takes everything out of me to get moving.
Do you often find yourself feeling restless or agitated, like you can't sit still?

Well, no, not restless at all. Like I was just saying, it's really the exact opposite of that. I don't have any trouble sitting still... in fact, sitting still is about all I seem to do these days. My husband, Arthur, he's the one who really pointed it out to me. He says I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm just dragging myself through molasses. 

I don't know if you heard me before, but I was telling you about the Piggly Wiggly... we go on Tuesdays for the senior discount, you know. And I was just standing there in the produce section, looking at the yellow onions. I knew I needed three of them for the pot roast, the medium ones, but I just stood there. Arthur had to come up and ask if we were going to wait for them to sprout! I just couldn't seem to make my arm reach out and grab them right away. There's this terrible delay, like my brain says 'go' and my body just says 'no, not yet.' 

So, no, I'm not agitated or fidgety or anything like that. If anything, I'm just so terribly slow, like every little movement is a chore. Even getting out of my recliner... it's a La-Z-Boy, sage green chenille... it takes me three or four tries just to get up. I just don't have that nervous energy you're talking about, not one bit.
Do you feel like your movements have slowed down significantly over the past four months?

Well, doctor, I feel like a broken record here, but yes, absolutely. Like I was just explaining a minute ago, my husband Arthur has been telling me for a while now—and it really has been about four months, right around the time the weather started turning—that I move like everything takes just so much extra effort. I am sure you heard me talking about the market just now, how I just stand there way too long before picking up what I came for. 

It is just... well, it is exhausting, honestly. Arthur will tell me it is like I am carrying a hundred pounds on my shoulders, and I suppose that is exactly how it feels. A few months ago, back in, oh, let us see, maybe late October or early November, I could still buzz around the kitchen, get the dishes put away, wipe down the counters... we have those Formica counters, you know, the ones that look like speckled granite but they are really just laminate, and they show every single little crumb if you do not wipe them down properly with a damp cloth. 

But now? Now I just stand there staring at the sponge by the sink. It is exactly like I was saying about the grocery store. I stand there too long before I can even make my hand reach out and do what I need to do. So, yes, it has definitely been a significant slowing down over these past few months, just like you said, and Arthur certainly has not been shy about pointing it out to me.
Do you often feel worthless or guilty about things that wouldn't have bothered you in the past?

Oh, the guilt... yes. It's funny you ask that, because it's been weighing on my mind so heavily lately, just sitting right here on my chest. It's mostly about my aunt. My Aunt Betty, she's my mother's younger sister. She's eighty-four now and lives over at the Shady Pines assisted living—it's a nice enough place, they have a lovely little courtyard with a birdbath, but she complains about the food constantly, says the Sunday meatloaf tastes like wet cardboard. 

Anyway, she calls me quite a bit, or she wants me to come visit and help her sort her mail or fix her television remote, and lately... well, with how exhausted I am, like I was telling you before, I just get so terribly annoyed with her. And I never used to be like that! I used to have all the patience in the world for Betty. But now, when I feel that tired or irritated by her calling right when I've finally managed to rock myself back in my chair, I get off the phone and I just start thinking that I am a downright bad woman. I really do. 

I sit there and think about how I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I mean, she's family, and she was so good to me when I was a little girl. She bought me my very first bicycle, a red one with a little white basket on the front, and she gave Arthur and me a beautiful silver-plated gravy boat for our wedding. And now I can't even muster the energy to listen to her talk about her arthritis without feeling resentful. 

And then the guilt just eats me alive, doctor. I feel so completely worthless for being such a bad niece. I start thinking about what my mother would say if she were still alive to see how ungrateful I'm being. Arthur tells me I'm being too hard on myself, that anyone would be tired, but I just can't shake this awful feeling that I'm a shameful disappointment. It just spins and spins in my head until I feel like I don't even deserve to be sitting in my own living room.
Do you find yourself feeling agitated or restless, like you're unable to sit still?

Doctor, I feel like I'm repeating myself here, but no, not restless. Not at all. Like I was saying just a little bit ago, it's really the exact opposite of being restless or agitated. I don't have any trouble sitting still... honestly, sitting still is about all I seem to manage these days. 

I know I already mentioned this, but my husband, Arthur, he's the one who really noticed it first. He tells me all the time that I move like everything takes so much extra effort now, like I'm walking through wet cement. And I was telling you about the grocery store, the Piggly Wiggly, right? I just stand there in the aisles. I stand there way too long before picking up what I came for, like my arm just won't listen to my brain. So no, no nervous energy or fidgeting. Just... terribly, terribly slow.
Do you feel like you're moving slower than you used to?

Well, yes, doctor, and I know we just touched on this, but it really is the truth. I am moving so much slower. I feel like a broken record, I really do, but like I was saying, Arthur—my husband—he's been pointing it out constantly. He says I move like every little thing takes just this monumental amount of extra effort. It's like I'm wading through molasses, you know? 

And I know I mentioned the grocery store earlier, but it really is the best example. I'll go down to the Piggly Wiggly to pick up just a few things, maybe some of those nice Roma tomatoes or a can of cream of mushroom soup for a casserole, and I'll just stand there in the aisle. I just stand there, staring at the shelves, way, way too long before I can even get my arm to reach out and pick up what I came for. It's not that I don't know what I want, it's just... the doing of it. The actual moving. It's just so terribly slow now. So yes, to answer your question, much, much slower than I ever used to be.
Do you find yourself pacing back and forth or engaging in other repetitive movements when you're feeling anxious or upset?

Doctor, I... well, I don't mean to be disrespectful, I really don't, but are you writing down what I'm saying? Because I feel like we are just going in circles here and I'm starting to wonder if I'm not speaking clearly enough. I don't pace. I couldn't pace if my life depended on it! Pacing takes energy, and like I keep trying to explain, I just don't have a drop of it. 

My husband, Arthur—like I've told you a few times already today—he says I move like everything takes extra effort now. Extra effort! Not nervous energy. He sees me trying to just get up from the floral sofa in our den, the one we bought over at the Sears before they closed it down, and he tells me it looks like a whole monumental chore just to stand up. And at the market—and I know I keep bringing up the Piggly Wiggly, but it really is the best way to explain it to you—I just stand there too long before picking up what I came for. 

I don't walk up and down the aisle, I don't tap my feet, I don't wring my hands... I just stand right there in one spot, staring at the groceries, trying to get my arm to work. Sometimes another shopper will even say "excuse me" to get past, and I realize I've been planted in the exact same spot on the linoleum for heaven knows how long. So no, no pacing back and forth, doctor. Just... stuck. I'm just terribly stuck.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling like you need to be in constant motion when you're sitting or lying down?

Doctor, I... I am really trying my best here, I truly am, but I just don't understand why we keep coming back to this same exact question. Have I done something wrong? Am I not explaining it right? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall, Lord forgive me for saying so. 

No, I do not fidget. I do not need to be in constant motion. When I am sitting down on my floral sofa, or lying in my bed with the blue quilt Arthur's mother made us, I am completely still. Almost like a statue, really. I just don't have the energy to move, let alone fidget. 

I know I've said this to you three times already today, but Arthur—he's my husband, we've been married almost forty years—he tells me all the time that I move like every single thing takes extra effort now. Even just lifting a spoon to my mouth or pulling the blankets up. It's not a nervous energy, it's a heaviness. A terrible, awful heaviness. And I know you've heard me say this, but even at the Piggly Wiggly, I just stand there in the aisle, looking at the cans of soup or the boxes of rice, and I stand there way, way too long before picking up what I came for. My body just doesn't want to move. So please, doctor, please try to hear me... I am not fidgety, I am not restless, and I certainly don't feel like I need to be in constant motion. I just want to sit still because moving is just too hard.
Do you feel like your symptoms have been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past four months?

Well, doctor, if you really want to know, and I suppose you do or you wouldn't have asked... I wouldn't say they're getting better. No, certainly not better. And maybe not exactly worse either, just... consistently heavy. Like a wet wool blanket that just won't dry out. 

But to answer your question about the timeframe, it's been about four months now. Yes, right around four months. I remember exactly because it all started right around the time my aunt—my mother's sister, Aunt Clara—came to live with us. She had a bad fall in her kitchen, broke her hip, and well, she just couldn't manage those stairs in her split-level anymore. Arthur and I, we have the ranch house over on Elm Street, so it just made sense for her to take our guest room. The one with the yellow wallpaper. 

Anyway, since she moved in, that's when this all really took hold. The slowness, the heaviness, the standing in the grocery store aisles like a fool... all of it. It's just been this constant, steady weight for these past four months. Not better, not worse, just... there. Every single day since Aunt Clara arrived with all her boxes and her orthopedic chair.
Are there things that you used to enjoy doing, but no longer find pleasure in?

Oh, doctor... yes. Yes, there are. And it really breaks my heart a little to even admit it out loud, but... well, I used to just love my watercolors. I have this beautiful little easel Arthur bought me for our thirty-fifth anniversary, the wooden kind that folds up, and I used to set it up right by the bay window in the front room. The morning light there is just perfect for painting the hydrangeas out front. But lately... lately I just leave my brushes and my little tubes of paint sitting right there on the sill. Aunt Clara even asked me the other day why I haven't painted her a picture yet, and I just looked at my things sitting there, gathering dust, and... I just can't make myself care. Not even a little bit. 

And it's not just the painting, either. It's the dance class I used to go to down at the community center on Tuesday nights. We had such a lovely time, tapping our feet to the music. And I used to go walking with the ladies from my church group every Thursday morning, too. We'd walk the loop around Centennial Park and then get a cup of Sanka at the diner. I used to look forward to my watercolors, dance class, and walking with the ladies so much! It was the highlight of my week, seeing everyone and catching up on all the neighborhood news. 

But now? I haven't been to dance class in months, and when the ladies call the house to see if I'm coming for the walk, I just have Arthur tell them I'm busy or that I'm resting on the sofa. I just don't have the heart for it anymore. I don't look forward to a single bit of it. Like I said, I just leave my things sitting there, and no matter how much I tell myself I ought to go out or pick up a brush, I just can't make myself care.

doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this way, with the heaviness and the thoughts about not wanting to wake up?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about four months, since my aunt came to live with us.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the symptoms (heaviness and thoughts about not wanting to wake up) have been present, which directly corresponds to the 'duration' item.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and look back at the calendar... I'd say it's been about four months now. Yes, four months. It all started right around the time my aunt came to live with us. You see, she just couldn't manage on her own anymore, bless her heart, and well, family is family, so of course we had to take her in. But oh, it was such a big adjustment for everyone. I really thought I could handle it just fine—I’ve always been the one to take care of things, you know? 

But right after she got settled in the spare room, that's when this... this awful heaviness just started creeping into my bones. At first, I honestly just thought I was worn out from moving all her boxes and rearranging the house. We had to move the whole living room around just to fit her favorite recliner, and I'm not as young as I used to be. But the heaviness, it never went away, it just got deeper and deeper. 

And then, maybe a few weeks after she moved in, that's when those nighttime thoughts started happening. So yes, four whole months of this. Four months of going to sleep just hoping I wouldn't have to do it all over again the next day. It’s a long time to feel like that, isn't it? I kept waiting to just bounce back like I used to, thinking maybe once we got into a routine with her it would lift, but the days just keep blurring together and that dark cloud just stays right there.

doctor.intent: determine presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these feelings started?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to my watercolors, dance class, and walking with the ladies, but lately I just leave my things sitting there and can't make myself care.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I still find pleasure in activities I used to enjoy, which directly corresponds to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, that's... that's a sad thing to admit, really. Because if you asked anyone who knows me, they'd tell you I used to be quite the busy bee. My days were just full of things I loved doing. Like my painting... I used to look forward to my watercolors so much. I have this little setup right by the kitchen window—the light hits just perfectly there in the late afternoons, you see, right around four o'clock. I'd paint little birds, mostly, or whatever flowers were blooming out front in the beds. I just loved mixing the colors on this little plastic palette I got at the craft store... but lately, I just... I just leave my things sitting there. The easel is still up, probably collecting dust by now, and I look at it and I just can't make myself care. It feels like such a mountain to climb just to think about filling up the little water cup. 

And it’s the exact same story with my dance class. Oh, I used to love Tuesday mornings! A group of us would go down to the community center for line dancing. We'd dance to those old country songs, and I even bought these special shoes with suede on the bottoms so you can slide real nice on the wood floor without scuffing it up. But now... I haven't been in months. I just look at those shoes sitting in the bottom of the closet and think, what's the point? I can't muster up a single ounce of joy for the music anymore, let alone the dancing. 

Even just walking with the ladies... I used to do that every Thursday, rain or shine, unless it was pouring, of course. We’d do a whole big loop around the park, catching up on all the neighborhood news, seeing whose grandkids were doing what, looking at the gardens. They still call me, bless them, they leave voicemails asking if I'm coming out with them, but I just let the phone ring. I tell myself I'll go, I really do, but then the time comes and... I just don't care about the walk, or the chatting, or any of it. It's just like all the color has washed right out of everything.

doctor.intent: determine presence of guilt or shame
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty about having these thoughts of not wanting to wake up?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: When I feel tired or annoyed with my aunt, I start thinking I'm a bad woman and that I'm bringing shame on my family for not being more grateful.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking if I feel guilty about my thoughts, which maps directly to the Worthlessness/Guilt symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, doctor, the guilt... the guilt is just awful. It really eats me alive. I do feel bad about those nighttime thoughts, yes, because I know how much that would hurt my family, but... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, the thing that really brings on the worst of the guilt, the thing that just makes me sick to my stomach, is how I've been feeling about my aunt. 

I mean, like I said before, family is family. My own mother, rest her soul, she always taught us that you take care of your own, no questions asked. You open your door. But lately, with this terrible heaviness making everything so hard... sometimes I just get so bone-tired, or I find myself getting just plain annoyed with her. She'll call out asking for a fresh glass of water, or she'll need help finding the television remote—she's always losing that little black remote down the side of the recliner cushions, you know, the one we had to move the whole room for—and I just feel this awful, ugly spike of irritation. 

And then, almost immediately, the guilt just crashes right down on me. I start thinking... I start thinking about what kind of a person I must be to feel that way. I tell myself I'm a bad woman. A truly bad, wicked woman for feeling annoyed at an elderly lady who just needs a little help and can't do for herself anymore. I feel like I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I mean, I should be counting my blessings! I should be grateful we have a nice home and a spare room to put her in, but instead, I'm just sitting there at the kitchen table feeling resentful. It’s shameful, it really is. I just sit there and think about how worthless I am for not having a better heart about it all, and how I'm failing everyone by being so ungrateful. It just loops in my head, over and over, how bad I am for feeling annoyed...

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past four months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant changes in weight, which corresponds to weight/appetite changes. My symptom profile does not include an item for weight changes.

patient.answer:
Well, my weight... you know, I haven't really stepped on the scale in a while. I used to keep it right there in the bathroom, tucked under the vanity, the one with the little blue dial that my husband bought me years ago. But honestly, I just haven't been paying much attention to it lately. I mean, my clothes seem to fit about the same, maybe a little looser or tighter depending on the day, but nothing that really makes me stop and think, "Oh, I've gained," or "Oh, I've lost." 

It's funny you ask, though, because I used to be so careful about my weight, especially back when I was going to my line dancing classes. I wanted to make sure I could still move around comfortably and not get too winded, you know? But now, with everything going on, with my aunt being here and all this heaviness I've been feeling, keeping track of my weight just hasn't even crossed my mind. I still cook, of course, because my aunt needs her three meals a day, and she’s quite particular about her breakfast—she has to have her oatmeal made with milk, not water, and just a tiny sprinkle of brown sugar. So I'm still in the kitchen, still putting food on the table, but as for me and my own weight... I just couldn't tell you if the numbers have moved one way or the other. I just haven't noticed any big changes, really.

doctor.intent: determine presence of sleep disturbance
doctor.question: Have you been having any trouble sleeping over the past four months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sleep disturbances (trouble sleeping), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sleep... oh, sleep has just been... well, it's just fine, really. I mean, I haven't noticed any real trouble with it. I go to bed around the same time I always do, usually right after the ten o'clock news finishes up. I like to watch the local broadcast, you know, just to see what the weather is going to do the next day, even though I hardly go out anymore. The meteorologist, the young man with the nice smile, he always does such a good job explaining the radar. Anyway, after that, I make sure the front door is locked, check that the stove is off—I have to check it two or three times just to be absolutely sure, a habit I picked up from my mother—and then I head to bed. 

And once I'm in bed, I just... I sleep. I guess I must be sleeping alright because I don't remember tossing and turning or waking up and looking at the clock at all hours of the night. My husband used to do that, bless him. He'd wake up at two in the morning and go sit in the living room and read his history books. But me, I just pull the covers up, and the next thing I know, it's morning and I have to get up to start the oatmeal for my aunt. So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble sleeping. It's just the usual routine, night in and night out, nothing out of the ordinary at all.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or feeling like it's harder to get things done physically over the past four months?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about moving more slowly or finding it physically harder to get things done, which directly maps to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have been moving a bit differently. My husband, bless his heart, he actually brought it up just the other day. We were in the kitchen, and I was trying to get the good china down from the top shelf of the hutch—the set we got for our 25th anniversary, the one with the little gold rim—and he came in and told me that I move like everything takes extra effort now. Like I'm walking through molasses or something. He said I look so heavy when I walk, like just lifting my feet is a chore. 

And, you know, I didn't want to admit it to him right then, because I don't want him worrying, but he's right. Even when I go to the market... oh, the market has become such an ordeal. I used to just zip in and out, you know? Grab my cart, go straight to the produce, pick out the firmest tomatoes, and be done with it. But lately, I'll go down to the Piggly Wiggly—I still go to the one on Elm Street because the produce manager, Mr. Henderson, always makes sure the apples are fresh—and I'll find myself just... standing there. I'll stand right in front of the display, looking at the fruit, and I just can't seem to make my hand reach out and pick up what I came for. It's like my brain knows what to do, but my body just takes so, so long to catch up. I just stand there for the longest time, staring, before I can finally get my arm to move and put a simple bag of carrots in the basket. It’s just so much harder to get anything done.

doctor.intent: determine presence of loss of energy
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have less energy than you used to?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: Even after a full night in bed, my body feels worn out, like carrying laundry or making breakfast takes more out of me than it should.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about having less energy, which corresponds to the symptom of fatigue.

patient.answer:
Energy... oh, my goodness, yes. It's just... I really don't know where it all went. Like I was telling you just a minute ago about my sleep, I spend a full night in bed, right? I get my rest, the whole night through, but when I wake up, my body just feels completely worn out. It just doesn't make any sense to me. I used to be up with the sun, ready to tackle the day, get the whole house in order before nine o'clock. 

But now... well, just making that breakfast I told you about, the oatmeal for my aunt, it takes so much out of me. I find myself having to lean against the kitchen counter while the milk heats up because I just don't have the strength to stand there straight. And the laundry! Oh, heavens, the laundry. I have this old wicker basket, the one with the little floral cloth liner that ties at the corners—my daughter bought it for me at a craft fair years ago, such a pretty thing—and just carrying that basket from the bedroom down the hall to the washing machine... it feels like I've run a marathon. It just takes more out of me than it ever should. I actually have to sit down on the edge of the bed and catch my breath before I can even think about pouring the detergent or sorting the whites from the colors. I just don't have the pep I used to have, no matter how much I sleep.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition has affected their appetite
doctor.question: Have you noticed any change in your appetite over the past four months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Appetite... well, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed much at all. I still eat my regular meals, just like always. It's funny you ask, though, because with how completely exhausted I feel, you'd think I just wouldn't have the stomach for it, but I still get hungry right on schedule. 

Like for breakfast... well, after I make that oatmeal for my aunt, I usually fix myself a slice of toast. Just one slice, usually the honey wheat, toasted right to a nice golden brown. I have this older toaster, a Sunbeam, the chrome kind—they just don't make them like that anymore, do they? It pops up perfect every single time. And I'll put a little butter on it, and maybe some of the strawberry preserves my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, brings over. She makes it from scratch every summer, boils the glass jars and seals them with the wax and everything. She's such a sweet lady, always checking in on me. 

And then for lunch, it's usually just a half a sandwich or a little bowl of soup. Campbell's tomato, mostly, especially when it's damp out. I'll heat it up on the stove—I just refuse to use the microwave for soup, it always gets boiling hot on the edges and stays ice cold in the middle, you know how that goes? And for dinner, well, I still try to make a proper meal, even if it takes me twice as long to stand there and chop the onions now because my arms feel so heavy. I'll do a nice meatloaf or a roast chicken. I always roast a chicken on Sundays, with the carrots and the little red potatoes all tucked around it in the pan to soak up the juices. 

So, yes, I'm still eating just about the exact same amount I always have. My stomach still rumbles right around noon, regular as a clock. I haven't noticed any difference at all in my appetite, really.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of concentration difficulties
doctor.question: Have you had trouble concentrating on things like reading or watching TV over the past four months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble concentrating or making decisions, which corresponds to diminished ability to think or concentrate. This symptom is not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Concentrating... well, let me think about that. No, I really haven't had any trouble with my concentration. I still watch my programs every evening just fine. My husband and I, we sit down right at 7:00 PM on the dot for Wheel of Fortune. We've been watching it for, oh, it must be thirty years now. Vanna always has the most beautiful gowns, doesn't she? I always tell my husband I'd love to know who her designer is, not that a woman my age has anywhere to wear a sequined floor-length dress! But I can follow the puzzles without any trouble at all. In fact, just last night, I solved the bonus puzzle before the contestant even guessed a vowel. It was 'A Walk in the Park.' So I can focus on that just perfectly. 

And as for reading, well, I don't read big thick novels so much, mostly because my eyes get a little tired with these bifocals if the print is too small, but I still read my Reader's Digest from cover to cover. My sister gets me a subscription every year for my birthday, she never forgets. They have those wonderful little stories, you know, the 'Drama in Real Life' section? I read one just yesterday afternoon about a man who got stuck in a terrible snowstorm in his pickup truck for three whole days up in the Dakotas somewhere. I read the entire article in one sitting while I was resting my legs on the sofa. I didn't lose my place or find myself having to reread paragraphs or anything like that. So, no, my mind is still sharp as a tack when it comes to paying attention to my shows and my magazines, even if my body is just dragging behind.

doctor.intent: Determine presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless, or do you feel like you're moving in slow motion most of the time?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling restless, fidgeting, or moving in slow motion, which directly corresponds to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Slow motion... well, it's funny you put it exactly that way, because that is exactly what my husband, Arthur, has been saying to me lately. He says I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm walking through molasses or something. And I suppose he's right, though I don't always notice it myself until he points it out. It's just... everything feels so heavy. 

Like the other day, we went down to the Piggly Wiggly—we always go on Tuesdays because they have the senior discount, ten percent off your whole cart, which really adds up when you're buying meat and coffee, you know? Anyway, we were in the produce section, and I needed to get some yellow onions for a pot roast I was planning to make. I like the medium-sized ones, not those giant Spanish onions, they're just too much for the two of us. And I was standing there, just standing in front of the onion bin, and Arthur came up behind me with the cart and said, "Martha, are you going to pick one or are we going to stand here until they sprout?" And I realized I had just been standing there... looking at them. For I don't know how long. I knew what I wanted, I knew I needed to reach out and put three of them in one of those little plastic bags on the roll, but I just... I couldn't seem to make my arm do it right away. 

It's like there's this delay between my brain telling my body to move and my body actually doing it. Even getting up from my recliner in the evening—it's a La-Z-Boy, the kind with the handle on the side, upholstered in this lovely sage green chenille—it takes me three or four tries to rock myself up, and then I just stand there for a minute before I take a step. I'm definitely not fidgety or restless, I can tell you that for sure. If anything, I'm just so terribly slow. It just takes everything out of me to get moving.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation, such as restlessness or an inability to sit still, which is a component of psychomotor changes.

Well, no, not restless at all. Like I was just saying, it's really the exact opposite of that. I don't have any trouble sitting still... in fact, sitting still is about all I seem to do these days. My husband, Arthur, he's the one who really pointed it out to me. He says I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm just dragging myself through molasses. 

I don't know if you heard me before, but I was telling you about the Piggly Wiggly... we go on Tuesdays for the senior discount, you know. And I was just standing there in the produce section, looking at the yellow onions. I knew I needed three of them for the pot roast, the medium ones, but I just stood there. Arthur had to come up and ask if we were going to wait for them to sprout! I just couldn't seem to make my arm reach out and grab them right away. There's this terrible delay, like my brain says 'go' and my body just says 'no, not yet.' 

So, no, I'm not agitated or fidgety or anything like that. If anything, I'm just so terribly slow, like every little movement is a chore. Even getting out of my recliner... it's a La-Z-Boy, sage green chenille... it takes me three or four tries just to get up. I just don't have that nervous energy you're talking about, not one bit.

doctor.intent: determine presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like your movements have slowed down significantly over the past four months?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a significant decrease in movements (psychomotor retardation), which directly maps to the Psychomotor_Changes symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I feel like a broken record here, but yes, absolutely. Like I was just explaining a minute ago, my husband Arthur has been telling me for a while now—and it really has been about four months, right around the time the weather started turning—that I move like everything takes just so much extra effort. I am sure you heard me talking about the market just now, how I just stand there way too long before picking up what I came for. 

It is just... well, it is exhausting, honestly. Arthur will tell me it is like I am carrying a hundred pounds on my shoulders, and I suppose that is exactly how it feels. A few months ago, back in, oh, let us see, maybe late October or early November, I could still buzz around the kitchen, get the dishes put away, wipe down the counters... we have those Formica counters, you know, the ones that look like speckled granite but they are really just laminate, and they show every single little crumb if you do not wipe them down properly with a damp cloth. 

But now? Now I just stand there staring at the sponge by the sink. It is exactly like I was saying about the grocery store. I stand there too long before I can even make my hand reach out and do what I need to do. So, yes, it has definitely been a significant slowing down over these past few months, just like you said, and Arthur certainly has not been shy about pointing it out to me.

doctor.intent: determine presence of worthlessness or guilt
doctor.question: Do you often feel worthless or guilty about things that wouldn't have bothered you in the past?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: When I feel tired or annoyed with my aunt, I start thinking I'm a bad woman and that I'm bringing shame on my family for not being more grateful.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of worthlessness or guilt, which matches the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, the guilt... yes. It's funny you ask that, because it's been weighing on my mind so heavily lately, just sitting right here on my chest. It's mostly about my aunt. My Aunt Betty, she's my mother's younger sister. She's eighty-four now and lives over at the Shady Pines assisted living—it's a nice enough place, they have a lovely little courtyard with a birdbath, but she complains about the food constantly, says the Sunday meatloaf tastes like wet cardboard. 

Anyway, she calls me quite a bit, or she wants me to come visit and help her sort her mail or fix her television remote, and lately... well, with how exhausted I am, like I was telling you before, I just get so terribly annoyed with her. And I never used to be like that! I used to have all the patience in the world for Betty. But now, when I feel that tired or irritated by her calling right when I've finally managed to rock myself back in my chair, I get off the phone and I just start thinking that I am a downright bad woman. I really do. 

I sit there and think about how I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I mean, she's family, and she was so good to me when I was a little girl. She bought me my very first bicycle, a red one with a little white basket on the front, and she gave Arthur and me a beautiful silver-plated gravy boat for our wedding. And now I can't even muster the energy to listen to her talk about her arthritis without feeling resentful. 

And then the guilt just eats me alive, doctor. I feel so completely worthless for being such a bad niece. I start thinking about what my mother would say if she were still alive to see how ungrateful I'm being. Arthur tells me I'm being too hard on myself, that anyone would be tired, but I just can't shake this awful feeling that I'm a shameful disappointment. It just spins and spins in my head until I feel like I don't even deserve to be sitting in my own living room.

I know I already mentioned this, but my husband, Arthur, he's the one who really noticed it first. doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving slower than you used to?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about moving slower, which directly relates to a decrease in psychomotor activity.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor, and I know we just touched on this, but it really is the truth. I am moving so much slower. I feel like a broken record, I really do, but like I was saying, Arthur—my husband—he's been pointing it out constantly. He says I move like every little thing takes just this monumental amount of extra effort. It's like I'm wading through molasses, you know? 

And I know I mentioned the grocery store earlier, but it really is the best example. I just stand there, staring at the shelves, way, way too long before I can even get my arm to reach out and pick up what I came for. It's not that I don't know what I want, it's just... the doing of it. The actual moving. It's just so terribly slow now. So yes, to answer your question, much, much slower than I ever used to be.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself pacing back and forth or engaging in other repetitive movements when you're feeling anxious or upset?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation (pacing, repetitive movements), which falls under psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... well, I don't mean to be disrespectful, I really don't, but are you writing down what I'm saying? Because I feel like we are just going in circles here and I'm starting to wonder if I'm not speaking clearly enough. I don't pace. I couldn't pace if my life depended on it! Pacing takes energy, and like I keep trying to explain, I just don't have a drop of it. 

My husband, Arthur—like I've told you a few times already today—he says I move like everything takes extra effort now. Extra effort! Not nervous energy. He sees me trying to just get up from the floral sofa in our den, the one we bought over at the Sears before they closed it down, and he tells me it looks like a whole monumental chore just to stand up. And at the market—and I know I keep bringing up the Piggly Wiggly, but it really is the best way to explain it to you—I just stand there too long before picking up what I came for. 

I don't walk up and down the aisle, I don't tap my feet, I don't wring my hands... I just stand right there in one spot, staring at the groceries, trying to get my arm to work. Sometimes another shopper will even say "excuse me" to get past, and I realize I've been planted in the exact same spot on the linoleum for heaven knows how long. So no, no pacing back and forth, doctor. Just... stuck. I'm just terribly stuck.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling like you need to be in constant motion when you're sitting or lying down?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My husband says I move like everything takes extra effort now, and even at the market I stand there too long before picking up what I came for.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about psychomotor agitation (fidgeting or needing to be in constant motion), which falls under psychomotor changes (S028).

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I am really trying my best here, I truly am, but I just don't understand why we keep coming back to this same exact question. Have I done something wrong? Am I not explaining it right? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall, Lord forgive me for saying so. 

No, I do not fidget. I do not need to be in constant motion. When I am sitting down on my floral sofa, or lying in my bed with the blue quilt Arthur's mother made us, I am completely still. Almost like a statue, really. I just don't have the energy to move, let alone fidget. 

I know I've said this to you three times already today, but Arthur—he's my husband, we've been married almost forty years—he tells me all the time that I move like every single thing takes extra effort now. Even just lifting a spoon to my mouth or pulling the blankets up. It's not a nervous energy, it's a heaviness. A terrible, awful heaviness. And I know you've heard me say this, but even at the Piggly Wiggly, I just stand there in the aisle, looking at the cans of soup or the boxes of rice, and I stand there way, way too long before picking up what I came for. My body just doesn't want to move. So please, doctor, please try to hear me... I am not fidgety, I am not restless, and I certainly don't feel like I need to be in constant motion. I just want to sit still because moving is just too hard.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving, worsening, or staying the same over time
doctor.question: Do you feel like your symptoms have been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past four months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about four months, since my aunt came to live with us.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression of my symptoms over the past four months, which corresponds to the duration of my current episode.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, if you really want to know, and I suppose you do or you wouldn't have asked... I wouldn't say they're getting better. No, certainly not better. And maybe not exactly worse either, just... consistently heavy. Like a wet wool blanket that just won't dry out. 

But to answer your question about the timeframe, it's been about four months now. Yes, right around four months. I remember exactly because it all started right around the time my aunt—my mother's sister, Aunt Clara—came to live with us. She had a bad fall in her kitchen, broke her hip, and well, she just couldn't manage those stairs in her split-level anymore. Arthur and I, we have the ranch house over on Elm Street, so it just made sense for her to take our guest room. The one with the yellow wallpaper. 

Anyway, since she moved in, that's when this all really took hold. The slowness, the heaviness, the standing in the grocery store aisles like a fool... all of it. It's just been this constant, steady weight for these past four months. Not better, not worse, just... there. Every single day since Aunt Clara arrived with all her boxes and her orthopedic chair.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are there things that you used to enjoy doing, but no longer find pleasure in?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to my watercolors, dance class, and walking with the ladies, but lately I just leave my things sitting there and can't make myself care.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about activities I used to enjoy but no longer find pleasure in, which maps directly to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, doctor... yes. Yes, there are. And it really breaks my heart a little to even admit it out loud, but... well, I used to just love my watercolors. I have this beautiful little easel Arthur bought me for our thirty-fifth anniversary, the wooden kind that folds up, and I used to set it up right by the bay window in the front room. The morning light there is just perfect for painting the hydrangeas out front. But lately... lately I just leave my brushes and my little tubes of paint sitting right there on the sill. Aunt Clara even asked me the other day why I haven't painted her a picture yet, and I just looked at my things sitting there, gathering dust, and... I just can't make myself care. Not even a little bit. 

And it's not just the painting, either. It's the dance class I used to go to down at the community center on Tuesday nights. We had such a lovely time, tapping our feet to the music. And I used to go walking with the ladies from my church group every Thursday morning, too. We'd walk the loop around Centennial Park and then get a cup of Sanka at the diner. I used to look forward to my watercolors, dance class, and walking with the ladies so much! It was the highlight of my week, seeing everyone and catching up on all the neighborhood news. 

But now? I haven't been to dance class in months, and when the ladies call the house to see if I'm coming for the walk, I just have Arthur tell them I'm busy or that I'm resting on the sofa. I just don't have the heart for it anymore. I don't look forward to a single bit of it. Like I said, I just leave my things sitting there, and no matter how much I tell myself I ought to go out or pick up a brush, I just can't make myself care.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of persistent feelings of sadness, loss of interest in activities, changes in appetite, sleep disturbances, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death have been present for at least four months, meeting the criteria for a Major Depressive Disorder.
